It should be noted that the Supreme Court of the United States has nothing in common with the French Cour de Cassation, since the latter hears appeals only on questions of law. The Supreme Court decides the facts of a case on the evidence as well as the law, whereas the Cour de Cassation does not give a decision of its own but sends the case to another tribunal for judgment. See the law of September 24, 1789, “Laws of the United States,” by Story, vol. i. p. 53.]

Means of Determining the Jurisdiction of the Federal Courts The difficulty of defining the jurisdiction of separate courts in confederations — The courts of the Union received the right to fix their own jurisdiction — In what way this rule infringes on the portion of sovereignty reserved to the several States — The sovereignty of these States is limited by the laws and by the interpretation of the laws — Hence the danger to the States is more apparent than real.

The Constitution of the United States recognized two distinct powers confronting each other, represented in the judicial sphere by two distinct classes of courts. Even the greatest care in defining their separate jurisdictions could not have prevented frequent collisions between those tribunals. The question then arose: who should have the right to decide the competence of each court?

In nations that form a single body politic, when two courts dispute their mutual jurisdiction, a third tribunal is generally at hand to settle the difference. This is done without difficulty, because in such nations questions of judicial competence have no bearing on the privileges of national supremacy. But it was impossible to create an arbiter between a superior court of the Union and the superior court of a separate State that would not itself belong to one of those two classes. It was therefore necessary to let one of the courts judge its own cause, and take or keep cognizance of the point in dispute. To grant this privilege to the courts of the States would have destroyed the sovereignty of the Union in fact after establishing it in law; for the interpretation of the Constitution would soon have given back to the States the very portion of independence that the terms of that act took from them. The purpose of creating a Federal tribunal was to stop the courts of the States from deciding, each in its own sphere, questions affecting national interests, and so to form a uniform body of jurisprudence for the interpretation of the laws of the Union. This purpose would not have been achieved if the courts of the several States had been competent to decide, in their separate capacities, cases from which they were obliged to abstain as Federal tribunals. The Supreme Court of the United States was therefore given the right to determine all questions of jurisdiction. *e

e [ To reduce the number of these suits, it was decided that in a great many Federal cases the courts of the States should have power to decide jointly with those of the Union, with the losing party having a right of appeal to the Supreme Court of the United States. The Supreme Court of Virginia disputed the right of the Supreme Court of the United States to judge an appeal from its decisions, but without success. See “Kent’s Commentaries,” vol. i. p. 300, pp. 370 et seq.; Story’s “Commentaries,” p. 646; and “The Organic Law of the United States,” vol. i. p. 35.]

This was a severe blow to the independence of the States, which was thus restricted not only by the laws but by the interpretation of them: by one limit that was known and another that was uncertain, by a rule that was fixed and a rule that was arbitrary. It is true that the Constitution laid down the precise limits of Federal supremacy, but whenever one of the States contests that supremacy, a Federal tribunal decides the question. Nevertheless, the dangers this procedure posed to the independence of the States are less serious than they appeared. We shall see later that in America the real strength of the country lies far more in the State governments than in the Federal government. The Federal judges are aware of the relative weakness of the power in whose name they act, and they are more inclined to give up a right of jurisdiction in cases where it is justly their own than to assert a privilege to which they have no legal claim.
Different Cases of Jurisdiction

The matter and the party are the first conditions of Federal jurisdiction — Suits in which ambassadors are involved — Suits of the Union — Of a separate State — By whom tried — Cases arising from the laws of the Union — Why they are judged by the Federal tribunals — Cases concerning the performance of contracts tried by the Federal courts — Consequence of this arrangement.

Having provided the means of fixing the competence of the Federal courts, the legislators of the Union defined the cases that should fall within their jurisdiction. They established, first, that certain parties must always be brought before the Federal courts, whatever the special nature of the case; and second, that certain kinds of cases must always be brought before those same courts, whatever the standing of the parties to the suit. These two distinctions were thus accepted as the basis of Federal jurisdiction.

Ambassadors are the representatives of nations at peace with the Union, and whatever concerns them concerns the whole Union to some degree. When an ambassador is a party to a suit, the suit affects the welfare of the nation, and it is natural that a Federal tribunal should be called on to decide it.

The Union itself may be a party to legal proceedings, and in that case it would be contrary both to the customs of all nations and to common sense to appeal to a tribunal representing any sovereignty other than its own; the Federal courts therefore take cognizance of these matters.

When two parties belonging to two different States are engaged in a suit, it would not be proper to bring the case before a court of either State. The surest course is to choose a tribunal like that of the Union, which neither party can suspect and which offers the most natural as well as the most certain remedy.

When the two parties are not private individuals but States, an important political consideration is added to the same motive of fairness. The standing of the parties gives national importance to all their disputes, and the most trifling litigation between States may be said to involve the peace of the whole Union. *f

f [ The Constitution also says that the Federal courts shall decide “controversies between a State and the citizens of another State.” Here a most important constitutional question arose: whether the jurisdiction given by the Constitution in cases where a State is a party extended to suits brought against a State as well as by it, or was confined exclusively to the latter. The question was examined at great length in the case of Chisholm v. Georgia, and the majority of the Supreme Court decided it in the affirmative. The decision caused general alarm among the States, and an amendment was proposed and ratified that removed the power entirely, as far as suits brought against a State are concerned. See Story’s “Commentaries,” p. 624, or in the large edition Section 1677.]

The nature of the case often determines which court is competent. Thus all questions concerning maritime commerce clearly fall within the cognizance of the Federal tribunals. *g Almost all these questions are connected with the interpretation of the law of nations, and in that respect they essentially concern the Union in its relations with foreign powers. Moreover, since the sea lies within the limits of no particular jurisdiction, the national courts are the only ones that can hear cases arising out of maritime affairs.
g [ For instance, all cases of piracy.]

The Constitution places under one head almost all the cases that by their very nature belong to the Federal courts. The rule it lays down is simple, but it carries within it an entire system of ideas and a vast multitude of facts. It declares that the judicial power of the Supreme Court shall extend to all cases in law and equity arising under the laws of the United States.
Two examples will show the intention of the legislator in the clearest light:

The Constitution prohibits the States from making laws on the value and circulation of money. Suppose that, despite this prohibition, a State passes such a law, and the interested parties refuse to comply with it because it is contrary to the Constitution. The case must come before a Federal court, because it arises under the laws of the United States. Again, if difficulties arise in collecting import duties voted by Congress, the Federal court must decide the case, because it turns on the interpretation of a law of the United States.

This rule is in perfect accordance with the fundamental principles of the Federal Constitution. The Union, as it was established in 1789, has, it is true, a limited supremacy; but it was intended that within its limits it should form one and the same people. *h Within those limits the Union is sovereign. Once this point is established and admitted, the inference is easy. If it is acknowledged that the United States constitute one and the same people within the bounds set by their Constitution, it is impossible to refuse them the rights that belong to other nations. But it has been accepted since the origin of society that every nation has the right to decide through its own courts the questions concerning the execution of its own laws. To this it is answered that the Union is in so singular a position that in relation to some matters it constitutes a people, and in relation to all the rest it is a nonentity. But the conclusion to be drawn is that, in the laws relating to those matters, the Union has all the rights of absolute sovereignty. The difficulty is to know what those matters are; and once that is resolved (and we have shown how it was resolved, in speaking of the means of determining the jurisdiction of the Federal courts), no further doubt can arise. For as soon as it is established that a suit is Federal — that is, that it belongs to the share of sovereignty reserved to the Union by the Constitution — the natural consequence is that it should come within the jurisdiction of a Federal court.

h [ This principle was restricted to some extent by the admission of the several States into the Senate as independent powers, and by allowing them to vote separately in the House of Representatives when the President is elected by that body. But these are exceptions, and the opposite principle is the rule.]

Whenever the laws of the United States are attacked, or whenever they are invoked in self-defense, the Federal courts must be appealed to. Thus the jurisdiction of the tribunals of the Union widens and narrows in exactly the same proportion as the sovereignty of the Union increases or decreases. We have shown that the principal aim of the legislators of 1789 was to divide the sovereign authority into two parts. In one they placed the control of all the general interests of the Union; in the other, the control of the special interests of its component States. Their chief concern was to arm the Federal government with enough power to resist, within its sphere, the encroachments of the several States. As for those communities, the principle adopted on their behalf was independence within certain limits of their own; they were shielded from the scrutiny, and protected from the control, of the central government. In speaking of the division of authority, I observed that this latter principle had not always been held sacred, since the States are prevented from passing certain laws that apparently belong to their own particular sphere of interest. When a State of the Union passes a law of this kind, the citizens injured by its execution can appeal to the Federal courts.

Thus the jurisdiction of the Federal courts extends not only to all the cases that arise under the laws of the Union, but also to those that arise under laws made by the several States in opposition to the Constitution. The States are forbidden to make ex post facto laws in criminal cases, and anyone condemned under such a law can appeal to the judicial power of the Union. The States are likewise forbidden to make laws that may tend to impair the obligation of contracts. *i If a citizen believes that such an obligation is impaired by a law passed in his State, he may refuse to obey it and may appeal to the Federal courts. *j

i [ It is perfectly clear, says Mr. Story (“Commentaries,” p. 503, or in the large edition Section 1379), that any law that enlarges, abridges, or in any manner changes the intention of the parties, as it results from the stipulations of the contract, necessarily impairs it. In the same place he gives a very long and careful definition of what Federal jurisprudence understands by a contract. A grant made by the State to a private individual and accepted by him is a contract, and cannot be revoked by any future law. A charter granted by the State to a company is a contract, and binds the State as much as the grantee. The clause of the Constitution referred to here therefore protects the existence of a great part of acquired rights, but not of all. Property may be legally held even though it did not pass into the possessor’s hands by means of a contract; and its possession is an acquired right that the Federal Constitution does not guarantee.]

j [ Mr. Story gives a remarkable instance of this (p. 508, or in the large edition Section 1388): “Dartmouth College in New Hampshire had been founded by a charter granted to certain individuals before the American Revolution, and its trustees formed a corporation under this charter. The legislature of New Hampshire had, without the consent of this corporation, passed an act changing the organization of the original provincial charter of the college, and transferring all the rights, privileges, and franchises from the old charter trustees to new trustees appointed under the act. The constitutionality of the act was contested, and, after solemn arguments, it was deliberately held by the Supreme Court that the provincial charter was a contract within the meaning of the Constitution (Art. I. Section 10), and that the emendatory act was utterly void, as impairing the obligation of that charter. The college was deemed, like other colleges of private foundation, to be a private eleemosynary institution, endowed by its charter with a capacity to take property unconnected with the Government. Its funds were bestowed upon the faith of the charter, and those funds consisted entirely of private donations. It is true that the uses were in some sense public, that is, for the general benefit, and not for the mere benefit of the corporators; but this did not make the corporation a public corporation. It was a private institution for general charity. It was not distinguishable in principle from a private donation, vested in private trustees, for a public charity, or for a particular purpose of beneficence. And the State itself, if it had bestowed funds upon a charity of the same nature, could not resume those funds.”]

This provision seems to me the most serious attack on the independence of the States. The rights granted to the Federal government for purposes of obvious national importance are definite and easy to understand; but the rights this last clause gives it can be neither clearly appreciated nor accurately defined. For there are vast numbers of political laws that affect the existence of obligations of contracts, and these may easily furnish a pretext for aggression by the central authority.
Procedure of the Federal Courts

Natural weakness of the judicial power in confederations — Legislators ought to strive as far as possible to bring private individuals, not States, before the Federal courts — How the Americans have succeeded in this — Direct prosecution of private individuals in the Federal courts — Indirect prosecution of the States that violate the laws of the Union — The decrees of the Supreme Court weaken but do not destroy the provincial laws.

I have shown what the privileges of the Federal courts are; it is no less important to point out how they are exercised. In countries where sovereignty is undivided, the irresistible authority of justice comes from the fact that the tribunals represent the entire nation in conflict with the individual against whom their decree is directed, so that the idea of power is added to support the idea of right. But this is not always the case in countries where sovereignty is divided. There the judicial power more often confronts a fraction of the nation than an isolated individual, and its moral authority and physical strength are consequently diminished. In federal States the power of the judge is naturally reduced, and that of the parties before the court is increased. In confederate States the legislator’s aim ought therefore to be to make the position of the courts similar to the one they hold in countries where sovereignty is undivided. In other words, his efforts ought constantly to tend to keep the judicial power of the confederation as the representative of the nation, and the party before the court as the representative of an individual interest.

Every government, whatever its constitution, needs the means to compel its subjects to discharge their obligations and to protect its privileges from their attacks. As far as the government’s direct action on the community is concerned, the Constitution of the United States contrived, by a master stroke of policy, that the Federal courts, acting in the name of the laws, should take cognizance only of parties in their individual capacity. For since it had been declared that the Union consisted of one and the same people within the limits laid down by the Constitution, the inference was that the government created by this Constitution, and acting within those limits, was invested with all the privileges of a national government, and one of the principal of these is the right to send its commands directly to the private citizen. When the Union votes a tax, for instance, it does not apply to the States to levy it, but to every American citizen in proportion to his assessment. The Supreme Court, which is empowered to enforce this law of the Union, exerts its influence not on a refractory State but on the private taxpayer; and, like the judicial power of other nations, it is set against the person of an individual. It should be observed that the Union chose its own opponent; and since that opponent is weak, he is naturally defeated.

But the difficulty increases when the proceedings are brought not by the Union but against it. The Constitution recognizes the legislative power of the States, and a law so enacted may impair the privileges of the Union. In that case a collision between the Union and the State that passed the law is unavoidable, and all that remains is to select the least dangerous remedy, which follows very clearly from the general principles I have already established. *k
k [ See Chapter VI. on “Judicial Power in America.”]

It might be thought that, in the case under consideration, the Union could have sued the State before a Federal court, which would have annulled the act; this would have been a natural course of proceeding. But the judicial power would then have been placed in open hostility to the State, and it was desirable to avoid that situation as far as possible. The Americans hold that it is nearly impossible for a new law not to impair the interests of some private individual by its provisions. American legislators take these private interests as the ground for attacking measures that may be prejudicial to the Union, and it is to such cases that the protection of the Supreme Court is extended.

Suppose a State sells a certain portion of its territory to a company, and a year later passes a law disposing of the territory in another way, so that the clause of the Constitution prohibiting laws that impair the obligation of contracts is violated. When the purchaser under the second act appears to take possession, the possessor under the first act brings his action before the tribunals of the Union and has the claimant’s title declared null and void. *l Thus in fact the judicial power of the Union is contesting the claims of a State’s sovereignty; but it acts only indirectly and on a special application in a particular case. It attacks the law in its consequences, not in its principle, and it weakens it rather than destroys it.
l [ See Kent’s “Commentaries,” vol. i. p. 387.]

The last possibility was that each State forms a corporation with a separate existence and distinct civil rights, and can therefore sue or be sued before a tribunal. Thus a State could bring an action against another State. In this instance the Union was not called on to contest a provincial law, but to try a suit in which a State was a party. This suit was perfectly similar to any other case, except that the parties were of a different standing; and here the danger pointed out at the beginning of this chapter is present, with less chance of being avoided. The inherent disadvantage, in the very essence of Federal constitutions, is that they give rise within the nation to parties that present powerful obstacles to the free course of justice.

High Rank of the Supreme Court Among the Great Powers of State No nation has ever created so great a judicial power as the Americans — Extent of its prerogative — Its political influence — The tranquility and the very existence of the Union depend on the discretion of the seven Federal judges.

When we have examined in turn the organization of the Supreme Court and all the prerogatives it exercises, we shall readily admit that no people has ever created a more imposing judicial power. The Supreme Court stands at the head of all known tribunals, both by the nature of its rights and by the class of parties over which it has jurisdiction.

In all the civilized countries of Europe the government has always shown the greatest reluctance to let cases in which it is itself a party be decided in the ordinary course of justice. This reluctance naturally reaches its height in an absolute government; and, on the other hand, the privileges of the courts widen as the people’s liberties increase. But no European nation has so far held that all judicial controversies, regardless of their origin, can be decided by the judges of common law.

In America this theory has actually been put into practice, and the Supreme Court of the United States is the sole tribunal of the nation. Its power extends to all cases arising under laws and treaties made by the executive and legislative authorities, to all cases of admiralty and maritime jurisdiction, and in general to all points that affect the law of nations. It may even be said that, although its constitution is essentially judicial, its prerogatives are almost entirely political. Its sole object is to enforce the execution of the laws of the Union; and the Union regulates only the relations of the government with the citizens and of the nation with foreign powers. The relations of citizens among themselves are regulated almost exclusively by the sovereignty of the States.

A second and still greater cause of this court’s preponderance can be given. In the nations of Europe the courts are called on to try only the controversies of private individuals; but the Supreme Court of the United States summons sovereign powers to its bar. When the clerk of the court steps forward and says simply, “The State of New York versus the State of Ohio,” one cannot help feeling that the court he addresses is no ordinary body. And when one recalls that one of these parties represents one million men and the other two million, one is struck by the responsibility of the seven judges whose decision is about to satisfy or disappoint so large a number of their fellow citizens.

The peace, the prosperity, and the very existence of the Union are in the hands of the seven judges. Without their active cooperation the Constitution would be a dead letter. The executive appeals to them for help against the encroachments of the legislative powers; the legislature asks their protection against the designs of the executive. They defend the Union against the disobedience of the States, the States against the exaggerated claims of the Union, the public interest against the interests of private citizens, and the conservative spirit of order against the fleeting innovations of democracy. Their power is enormous, but it is clothed in the authority of public opinion. They are the all-powerful guardians of a people that respects the law, but they would be powerless against popular neglect or popular contempt. The force of public opinion is the most intractable of agents, because its exact limits cannot be defined; and it is no less dangerous to exceed the boundary it prescribes than to fall short of it.

The Federal judges must not only be good citizens, and men with the knowledge and integrity indispensable to magistrates; they must also be statesmen. They must be politicians, well read in the signs of the times, unafraid to face obstacles that can be overcome, and not slow to turn aside any encroaching forces that may threaten the supremacy of the Union and the obedience due to the laws.

The President, who exercises a limited power, may err without doing great harm to the State. Congress may decide wrongly without destroying the Union, because the electorate from which Congress originates can make it reverse its decision by changing its members. But if the Supreme Court is ever composed of imprudent men or bad citizens, the Union may be plunged into anarchy or civil war.

The real cause of this danger, however, lies not in the constitution of the tribunal but in the very nature of Federal governments. We have observed that in confederate peoples it is especially necessary to consolidate the judicial authority, because in no other nations are the independent individuals who can cope with the social body so powerful, or so well placed to resist the physical strength of the government. But the more a power needs to be strengthened, the more extensive and independent it must be made, and the dangers its abuse may create grow with its independence and strength. The source of the evil is therefore not in the constitution of the power but in the constitution of the States that make its existence necessary.
In What Respects the Federal Constitution Is Superior to That of the States

In what respects the Constitution of the Union can be compared to those of the States — The superiority of the Constitution of the Union is due to the wisdom of the Federal legislators — The legislature of the Union is less dependent on the people than those of the States — The executive power is more independent in its sphere — The judicial power is less subject to the inclinations of the majority — Practical consequence of these facts — The dangers inherent in a democratic government were avoided by the Federal legislators and increased by the legislators of the States.

The Federal Constitution differs essentially from those of the States in the ends it is meant to achieve, but in the means by which those ends are pursued there is a closer resemblance. The objects of the governments are different, but their forms are the same; and from this particular point of view there is some advantage in comparing them.
I am of the opinion that the Federal Constitution is superior to all the Constitutions of the States, for several reasons.

The present Constitution of the Union was formed later than those of most of the States, and it may have gained some improvements from past experience. But we shall be led to acknowledge that this is only a secondary cause of its superiority, when we recall that eleven new States *n have been added to the American Confederation since the Federal Constitution was promulgated, and that these new republics have always exaggerated rather than avoided the defects of the earlier Constitutions.
n [ [The number of States has now risen to 46 (1874), besides the District of Columbia.]]

The chief cause of the Federal Constitution’s superiority lay in the character of the legislators who composed it. When it was formed, the dangers facing the Confederation were imminent and its ruin seemed inevitable. In this extremity the people chose the men who most deserved the country’s esteem, rather than those who had won its affections. I have already observed that, distinguished as almost all the legislators of the Union were for their intelligence, they were still more distinguished for their patriotism. They had all been raised at a time when the spirit of liberty was strengthened by a continual struggle against a powerful and dominant authority. When the contest ended, the excited passions of the populace persisted in fighting dangers that had ceased to threaten them, but these men stopped short in their course. They cast a calmer and more penetrating look on their country, which was now their own. They saw that the war of independence was definitely over, and that the only dangers America had left to fear were those that might result from abuse of the freedom she had won. They had the courage to say what they believed to be true, because they were animated by a warm and sincere love of liberty; and they ventured to propose restrictions, because they were resolutely opposed to destruction. *o
o [ At this time Alexander Hamilton, one of the principal founders of the Constitution, ventured to express the following views in “The Federalist,” No. 71:

“There are some who would be inclined to regard the servile pliancy of the Executive to a prevailing current, either in the community or in the Legislature, as its best recommendation. But such men entertain very crude notions, as well of the purposes for which government was instituted as of the true means by which the public happiness may be promoted. The Republican principle demands that the deliberative sense of the community should govern the conduct of those to whom they entrust the management of their affairs; but it does not require an unqualified complaisance to every sudden breeze of passion, or to every transient impulse which the people may receive from the arts of men who flatter their prejudices to betray their interests. It is a just observation, that the people commonly intend the public good. This often applies to their very errors. Most of the Constitutions of the States set the term of the House of Representatives at one year and that of the Senate at two, so that members of the legislative body are constantly and narrowly tied down by the slightest wishes of their constituents. The legislators of the Union held that this excessive dependence of the legislature tended to alter the nature of the main consequences of the representative system, since it placed the source, not only of authority but of government, in the people. They lengthened the term for which representatives are returned, to give them freer scope to exercise their own judgment.

The Federal Constitution, like the Constitutions of the different States, divided the legislative body into two branches. But in the States the two branches were composed of the same elements and elected in the same manner. The consequence was that the passions and inclinations of the populace were as rapidly and as energetically represented in one chamber as in the other, and that laws were made with all the marks of violence and haste. Under the Federal Constitution the two houses likewise originate in the choice of the people, but the conditions of eligibility and the mode of election were changed. The purpose was that, if one branch of the legislature represents the same interests as the other, as happens in certain nations, it may at least represent a higher degree of intelligence and discretion. A mature age was made one of the conditions for the senatorial dignity, and the upper house was chosen by an elected assembly of limited numbers.

To concentrate the whole social force in the hands of the legislative body is the natural tendency of democracies. For since this is the power that emanates most directly from the people, it is made to share most fully in the preponderant authority of the multitude, and it is naturally led to monopolize every kind of influence. This concentration is at once harmful to well-conducted administration and favorable to the despotism of the majority. The legislators of the States frequently yielded to these democratic propensities, which the founders of the Union invariably and courageously resisted.

In the States the executive power is vested in a magistrate who is apparently placed on a level with the legislature, but who is in reality nothing more than the blind agent and passive instrument of its decisions. He can gain no influence from the length of his term, which ends with the turning year, or from the exercise of prerogatives, which can scarcely be said to exist. The legislature can condemn him to inaction by entrusting the execution of the laws to special committees of its own members, and can annul his temporary dignity by depriving him of his salary. The Federal Constitution vests all the privileges and all the responsibility of the executive power in a single individual. The term of the Presidency is fixed at four years; the salary of the person who holds that office cannot be altered during his term; he is protected by a body of official dependents and armed with a suspensive veto. In short, every effort was made to give the executive authority a strong and independent position within the limits prescribed to it.

In the Constitutions of all the States the judicial power is the one that remains most independent of the legislative authority. Nevertheless, in all the States the legislature has reserved to itself the right to regulate the judges’ salaries, a practice that necessarily subjects these magistrates to its immediate influence. In some States the judges are appointed only temporarily, which deprives them of a great part of their power and freedom. In others the legislative and judicial powers are entirely confounded; the Senate of New York, for instance, constitutes in certain cases the Superior Court of the State. The Federal Constitution, on the other hand, carefully separates the judicial authority from all outside influences, and it provides for the independence of the judges by declaring that their salary shall not be altered and that their office cannot be taken from them.
